title: Virtual memory
objectives: Explain pages, the TLB and a page fault, and what each costs.

screens.title: Translate one address
screens.prose: A program never sees physical memory. Its addresses are virtual: a page number, then an offset inside the page. The **page table** maps each page to a physical frame.
screens.question: Translate virtual address 0x2A7C (10,876). What is the physical address? Answer in decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the address into page and offset first.

byKey.frame: 36,864 is the start of frame 9. Add the offset 2,684.
byKey.same: The virtual address has to be translated through the table.
byKey.offset: 2,684 is only the offset. Add the frame's start.
byKey.frame7: You used frame 7, which belongs to page 0. Byte 10,876 is in page 2.

explain.text: Page 2, offset 2,684. Page 2 lives in frame 9, so $9 \times 4{,}096 + 2{,}684 = 39{,}548$. The offset never changes; only the page number is swapped for a frame.

screens.title: A page that is not there
screens.prose: Slide the virtual address and watch the translation. Pages 0 and 2 have frames; page 1 has none yet.

derive.caption: {{frames[floor(v.x / 4096)] < 0 ? 'Address ' + v.x + ' is in page 1, which is not present.' : 'Address ' + v.x + ': page ' + floor(v.x / 4096) + ', offset ' + (v.x - 4096 * floor(v.x / 4096)) + ', physical ' + (frames[floor(v.x / 4096)] * 4096 + (v.x - 4096 * floor(v.x / 4096))) + '.'}}

screens.question: Slide to 4,096 (0x1000). What happens to a read there?

options.text: A page fault, handled by the kernel

options.why: Page 1 has no frame yet, so there is nothing to read.
A fault is not a crash. The kernel handles it and the read retries.
Physical addresses come from the page table, never straight from the virtual one.

hints.text: 4,096 is the first byte of page 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look up page 1 in the table.

explain.text: Page 1 has no frame, so the hardware raises a **page fault**. The kernel finds a frame, fills in the table and retries the read. A minor fault costs about 1 µs; one that loads from an SSD costs about 100 µs.

screens.title: Four levels
screens.prose: x86-64 uses 48-bit virtual addresses. The low 12 bits are the offset in a 4 KiB page. The rest are four 9-bit indexes, one per level of the page table.
screens.question: Write each part in decimal.

hints.text: Read each group of bits as a binary number.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Convert each binary group on its own.

explain.text: Each index picks one entry at its level, and the offset 0xE48 is 3,656. Every level is one more memory read. A full walk can cost $4 \times 100 = 400$ ns when none of it is cached.

screens.title: The TLB
screens.prose: Walking four levels on every read would be slow. So the core keeps recent translations in the **TLB**, the translation lookaside buffer.

params.title: One core
lines: TLB: 64 entries, one page translation each
page size: 4 KiB (or 2 MiB with huge pages)
table: 64 MiB, read at random positions

screens.question: Fill in the reach and the hit rate.

rows: Chance a random read finds its page in the TLB

hints.text: Reach is entries times page size.
64 MiB is $2^{26}$ bytes and 4 KiB is $2^{12}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

explain.text: 64 entries of 4 KiB reach 256 KiB, so random reads over 64 MiB hit only 0.39%. With 2 MiB pages the table is 32 pages, all inside a reach of 128 MiB. These are **huge pages**.

screens.title: Write the translation
screens.prose: Now in code. `frames[p]` is page p's frame, or −1 when page p is not mapped. Pages are 4,096 bytes.
screens.question: Fix `translate` so it returns the physical address, or −1 for a page fault.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Ten hidden tests. They include the first and last byte of a page, a missing page and an empty table.

hints.text: What does the starter forget to add?
The offset is `vaddr % 4096`, and a frame of −1 is a fault.

feedback.correct: That's it. Split, check, then rebuild the address.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

explain.text: The starter drops the offset and reads frame −1 as a real frame. A missing page must return −1 before any arithmetic. Page past the table and page not present are both faults.

screens.title: When does 1 GiB cost 262 ms
screens.prose: A desk program on a Linux server asks for 1 GiB and fills it. It takes about 262 ms longer than the writes alone. This app runs in WebAssembly, which has no page faults to show.
screens.question: Where is the 262 ms spent?

options.text: In the loop: one page fault per 4 KiB page, on first write
In `new`: the kernel finds 1 GiB of frames at the call
options.why: The kernel only reserves addresses; frames arrive when a page is first touched.
Freeing touches nothing, so it is cheap.

options.text: In cache misses during the loop
options.why: Sequential writes stream through the cache. 262 ms is 262,144 faults at 1 µs.

hints.text: What does `new` actually get from the kernel?
Addresses are reserved at once; frames are not.
1 GiB is 262,144 pages, and each first write faults.

feedback.correct: In the loop: 262,144 faults at about 1 µs each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask when each page first gets a frame.

byKey.b: Most of the cost is not at the call. The kernel hands out frames lazily, one fault per page.

explain.text: `new` reserves 1 GiB of virtual addresses and returns at once. The first write to each of 262,144 pages faults. At about 1 µs a fault, that is 262 ms inside the loop.

screens.title: Bigger than RAM
screens.prose: Virtual space is per process, and only touched pages need frames. A 48-bit address can name a lot of bytes.
screens.question: How many TiB can a 48-bit virtual address name?

feedback.correct: 256 TiB, far more than any server's RAM.

byKey.tb: 281 is in decimal terabytes. A TiB is $2^{40}$ bytes.
byKey.bits: 48 is the number of bits, not the size.
byKey.gib: 262,144 is in GiB. Divide by 1,024 again.

explain.text: $2^{48}$ bytes is 256 TiB, so the space is far bigger than RAM. Each process has its own table. Two processes can use one virtual address for different frames.

screens.title: Every read, in order
screens.prose: Put the steps of one read into order. One line does not belong.
screens.question: Order the steps of a read through virtual memory, and leave out the wrong one.

lines.text: Split the address into a page number and an offset
Look the page up in the TLB
On a TLB miss, walk the page table
If the page is not present, fault: the kernel supplies a frame and the read retries
Form the physical address: frame × 4,096 + offset
Ask the kernel to translate the address
lines.why: The hardware translates every access. The kernel only steps in on a fault.

hints.text: What does the hardware need before it can look anything up?
The TLB comes before the walk; the walk finds the fault.
Split, TLB, walk, fault if needed, then frame times 4,096 plus offset.

feedback.correct: That's it: split, TLB, walk, fault, address.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The cheap check comes before the expensive one.

byKey.d1: A system call per read would cost far more than the read. The hardware does the translation.
byKey.left-out: Every one of the five hardware steps belongs in the order.
byKey.s3: The walk only happens when the TLB has no entry for the page.

explain.text: The TLB is checked first because it costs almost nothing. A miss costs a walk of up to four reads. A page that is not present costs a fault, which is far dearer.

screens.title: The translation
screens.prose:
Every translation today was the same three lines:

$$p = \left\lfloor \frac{v}{4{,}096} \right\rfloor, \qquad o = v \bmod 4{,}096$$

$$\text{physical} = \text{frame}(p) \times 4{,}096 + o$$

A page with no frame is a fault.
screens.question: Frames [7, none, 9]. Where does virtual address 8,195 go?

options.why: You used frame 7, which is page 0's. 8,195 is in page 2.
8,195 is in page 2, which is present. Page 1 is the missing one.
A virtual address must be translated; it is not the physical one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split 8,195 into page and offset.

screens.title: Drill: pages
screens.prose: Drill: about 90 seconds each. Say the reasoning aloud first. Pages are 4 KiB unless stated. Fault and walk costs are round figures: know them to a power of ten, not to the digit.
screens.question: Fill in each answer.

rows: 0x3B10 (15,120) with frames [5, 2, none, 8]: physical address in decimal
0x2000 (8,192), same table: physical address, or −1 for a fault
Faults on first touch of 3 GiB

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r1c1: Page 2 has no frame, so it faults.

explain.text: Each address answer is split, look up, rebuild. Each size answer is a ratio of powers of two. Say the page size aloud before you divide.

screens.title: Follow-up: start-up
screens.prose: Why does a trading process touch and lock all its memory at start-up? It moves 786 ms of faults out of the session. It also removes 1 µs stalls from the hot path.

params.title: Start-up of a trading process
lines: map 3 GiB for books and buffers
write every page: 786,432 faults, about 786 ms
lock the pages so they stay in RAM
market opens: no page faults on the hot path

screens.question: With 2 MiB huge pages, how many pages hold 3 GiB?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 3 GiB by 2 MiB.

byKey.small: 786,432 is the count of 4 KiB pages.

explain.text: 3 GiB is 3,072 MiB, so 1,536 huge pages, 512 times fewer than 786,432. A 1,536-entry TLB holding 2 MiB entries would then cover all of it. Desks pre-fault, lock and use huge pages for this.

ideas: A virtual address is a page number and an offset; the page table swaps the page for a frame.
The TLB caches recent translations; a miss costs a walk of up to four reads, about 400 ns.
A page gets a frame when first touched. The fault costs about 1 µs, or 100 µs from an SSD.

formula.name: Translation
formula.note: No frame means a page fault.

summary.trap: Thinking `new` pays for its memory at the call: the faults come on first touch.

quiz.prose: A trading process writes every page of its 3 GiB heap, then locks it, before the market opens.
quiz.question: Why?

options.text: To take every page fault before trading starts
To use less memory during the session
options.why: Touching every page makes all of it resident at once.

options.text: Because the kernel requires it for large heaps
options.why: The kernel would fault pages in on demand.

options.text: To fill the CPU caches before the open
options.why: 3 GiB is far bigger than any cache.

feedback.correct: To move the faults out of the session.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What would happen on the first touch during trading?

explain.text: Each first touch costs a fault of about 1 µs. Doing all 786,432 before the open keeps them off the hot path. Locking stops the kernel from taking frames back.

quiz.question: What is the physical address of virtual 4,100?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. 4,100 is page 1, offset 4.

byKey.frame3: Frame 3 belongs to page 0. 4,100 is in page 1.
byKey.same: The address has to be translated.

quiz.prose: A TLB of 32 entries, pages of 4 KiB.
quiz.question: What is its reach, in KiB?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the entries by the page size.

byKey.bytes: 131,072 is in bytes. The question asks for KiB.

explain.text: $32 \times 4$ KiB is 128 KiB. Reads spread over more than that miss the TLB.

quiz.prose: A program first touches 512 MiB with 4 KiB pages. Each minor fault costs about 1 µs.
quiz.question: How long do the faults take, in ms?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pages first.

byKey.pages: 131,072 is the count of faults. Each takes 1 µs.
